extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators and appellate judges (Supreme Court / Federal Circuit), patent examiners, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: A Supreme Court petition arguing that Alice/Mayo §101 jurisprudence must be clarified to distinguish eligibility from novelty/obviousness, and criticizing the Federal Circuit's summary Rule 36 affirmances. It frames legal standards for when devices/systems are patent-eligible and when §101 should not be used to decide disputed factual questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 101 statutory text
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. § 101 provides: 'Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the text of § 101 as the starting point for eligibility analysis and remember it is 'subject to the conditions and requirements' of the patent statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Step one: determine whether the claim is 'directed to' a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea). Step two: if so, determine whether the claim contains an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent in practice amounts to 'significantly more' than the ineligible concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the two-step test, courts should focus on the language of § 101 itself and avoid conflating the inquiry with novelty/obviousness/enablement analyses under §§ 102, 103, and 112. The Court quoted Alice: transformation into a patent-eligible application requires more than simply stating the abstract idea while adding the words 'apply it'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate novelty/obviousness/enablement from eligibility (Diehr distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty under § 102, non-obviousness under § 103, and written description/enablement under § 112 are distinct inquiries from § 101 eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Diamond v. Diehr: whether an invention is novel is 'wholly apart from whether the invention falls into a category of statutory subject matter.' Courts should not resolve § 102/103/112 factual questions within the § 101 eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be considered 'as a whole'
rubrics_metrics.description: The § 101 inquiry must focus on the claims as a whole rather than abstracting to a high-level concept not reflected in the claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not frame the 'abstract idea' at an overbroad level of generality untethered from the actual claim limitations; follow Diehr and Parker v. Flook in examining the claim language and its specific limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement: 'significantly more' than the abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: To survive § 101 step two, claims must recite an 'inventive concept' — something more than the abstract idea that ensures the claimed invention in practice amounts to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventive concept cannot be merely the application of the abstract idea using 'well-understood, routine, conventional' activity. Courts should look for technical improvements, specific arrangements, or other limitations that convert an abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Well-understood, routine, conventional' determinations are factual
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether elements of a claim are 'well-understood, routine, or conventional' is often a question of fact that can turn on the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Cellspin, Berkheimer, and related authority, factual disputes about conventionality should normally be resolved on the merits (not on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion). If a plaintiff pleads plausible factual allegations that particular implementations were not conventional, the court must accept those allegations at the pleading stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifications are not admissions that claim elements are conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent specifications are drafted for § 112 written-description/enablement purposes and should not be treated as admissions that claimed components were 'conventional' or 'well-understood.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should not use boilerplate or explanatory language in the specification as conclusive evidence that claimed components are conventional; such reliance risks conflating § 112/§101/§102 analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered combination of conventional components can be inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventive combination may arise from arranging known physical components in a new and useful ordered combination (e.g., specific arrangement that converts signals parallel-to-serial, analog-to-digital, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if individual components are conventional, their novel arrangement or integration into a machine/apparatus that achieves a technical result can supply the requisite inventive concept under § 101; the radio example is used to illustrate this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test as a 'useful and important clue'
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test is a relevant indicator for determining patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not dispositive, presence of a claimed machine or transformation (e.g., Diehr/Bilski guidance) supports eligibility analysis and helps distinguish patentable inventions from abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid high-level abstract-idea characterizations untethered to claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should not invalidate claims by characterizing them at an overly high level of abstraction (e.g., 'collecting, analyzing, manipulating, and displaying data') when the claims recite specific apparatus features and operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'abstract idea' formulation must be tied to the claim language; inventors may claim concrete interfaces or operations (like icons tied to specific operations) that are not equivalent to mere data-display abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern: do not let the abstract-idea exception 'swallow all of patent law'
rubrics_metrics.description: An eligibility rule that invalidates inventions in a way that preempts use of basic tools of scientific and technological work undermines patent law's purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Alice's admonition: ensure that § 101 doctrine does not prohibit patents that claim concrete technological solutions and thus 'swallow all of patent law.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleadings standard on §101 motions — specific, plausible factual allegations required
rubrics_metrics.description: On a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, plaintiffs must allege specific, plausible factual allegations about inventive concepts or non-conventional implementations to survive dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must accept well-pled factual allegations and not dismiss as merely conclusory statements that claim elements are inventive; quoting claims/spec may be insufficient without context showing non-conventional implementation (Cellspin, Aatrix, Am. Bankers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit invalidity rulings to asserted claims rather than entire patents
rubrics_metrics.description: When adjudicating eligibility, courts should confine invalidity determinations to the specific asserted claims rather than invalidating entire patents wholesale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petition criticizes the Claims Court for applying its § 101 ruling to the entirety of the patents rather than to particular asserted independent claims; best practice is to cabin rulings to the claims at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate decisionmaking: reasoned opinions preferred over Rule 36 one-word affirmances
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary affirmances (Federal Circuit Rule 36) produce no reasoned precedent and undermine the Federal Circuit's role in articulating uniform patent law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When cases raise unsettled or complex issues of patent law, appellate courts should issue reasoned opinions (or rehear en banc) to provide guidance and uniformity rather than repeatedly issuing one-word 'affirmed' judgments.
